abstracts.value: Data-driven machine learning algorithms represent an alternative to numerical or analytical modeling of vibrating objects for the purpose of extracting their material or geometric properties. Their performance is conditioned by the quality of the training dataset, which should contain all possible production configurations of the object and measurement conditions. In this work, we propose a data-augmentation method based on manipulations of the vibration properties rather than numerical signal post-processing. Instead of modifying the sample’s material or geometry, we connect an additional sensor and actuator to the sample and use low-latency electronics to control the feedback signal. This delivers an electromechanical system with tunable oscillation properties. This signal diversification method is demonstrated on the classification of correct and incorrect adhesion of two aluminum plates. The labeling accuracy of 67% on nine unknown test objects, when trained on a single unchangeable training object, increases to 83% when the variety of the training vibration signals is augmented by varying the parameters of the electrovibratory feedback. This provides advantages for industrial quality control, where a large number of reference training samples are not available.

titles.title: Data augmentation by an electro-vibratory feedback improves signal interpretation by neural networks

abstracts.value: A new quench-protection technique, energy shift with coupling (ESC), has recently been proposed and shows significant promise for the protection of high-field magnets. The ESC system includes normal-conducting coils that are strongly magnetically coupled to, but galvanically insulated from, the magnet coils. When activated, the system rapidly transfers energy from the magnet to the ESC coils, substantially reducing ohmic losses at the magnet hot spot and promoting the transition of the superconducting coils to the normal state through transient losses. During the subsequent magnet-current discharge, part of the stored magnetic energy is transferred to the ESC coils. ESC was recently demonstrated successfully at CERN on a 400 mm long flat racetrack magnet structure without an aperture. In this work, we present the application of the ESC method to a subscale common-coil magnet known as the subscale stress-managed common-coil series (subSMCC2), designed and manufactured by the Magnet Development Laboratory at the Paul Scherrer Institute. The subSMCC2 is a 300 mm long magnet comprising four stress-managed Nb₃Sn common coils and is designed to reach bore and peak coil fields of approximately 5.3 T and 6.4 T, respectively, at a short-sample current of 9.5 kA. Protecting this magnet following a quench, without the use of energy extraction, is particularly challenging because of its very high stabilizer current density, exceeding 5 kA/mm². The proposed ESC-based protection scheme employs two common-coil-type ESC coils made from rectangular copper conductors and located on the outer sides of the magnet coils. Tests performed at the CERN magnet test facility successfully demonstrated the performance of the ESC system under a variety of operating conditions. These results show that ESC is an effective, high-performance quench-protection technology capable of protecting magnets operating at very high current densities.

titles.title: ESC Enables Protection of an Accelerator Superconducting Magnet With $>$5 kA/mm$^{2}$ Copper Current Density

abstracts.value: Realistic simulation of quantum key distribution (QKD) networks requires a combination of precise models of quantum channels and network functions. Unfortunately, existing QKD network simulators lack either rigorous quantum physics modeling or network key-management and routing protocols, which limit their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose a QKD network simulator with hyperparameter tuning (QKDSim-HT), a NetSquid-based simulator specialized for polarization-based discrete-variable QKD networks. Specifically, QKDSim-HT models properties in quantum physics (photon loss, polarization-dependent depolarization, detector inefficiencies, dark counts, and dead times) as well as advanced functionalities in networking algorithms (multi-hop key relay and adaptive routing). Extensive simulations over diverse topologies reveal that the networking performance varied with respect to the fundamental properties of quantum physics, such as depolarization, fiber length, and channel attenuation. As a representative use case of QKDSim-HT, simulation results from QKDSim-HT over simple examples clearly manifest that a design of QKD networks highly affects performance of the networks. Accordingly, QKDSim-HT can serve as a practical platform for performance evaluation and optimization of quantum secured network.

titles.title: Quantum Key Distribution Network Simulator With Hyperparameter Tuning for Realistic Performance Analysis

abstracts.value: We present a unified theoretical framework for analyzing both electrostatic two-stream and electromagnetic Weibel instabilities in counterstreaming electron-positron pair plasmas. Through systematic derivation of dispersion relations in non-relativistic and relativistic regimes, we demonstrate how the symmetric mass ratio fundamentally alters instability characteristics compared to electron-ion systems. The two-stream instability, driven by longitudinal electrostatic perturbations parallel to beam motion, exhibits enhanced growth rates in pair plasmas due to equal contributions from both species, with relativistic suppression scaling as γ0−3 for both electrons and positrons. The Weibel instability, arising from transverse electromagnetic modes perpendicular to streaming directions, lacks the heavy-ion stabilization present in electron-ion plasmas, producing broader unstable spectral ranges and modified saturation levels. We derive explicit conditions determining the relative dominance of each mechanism across parameter space defined by drift velocity, wavenumber orientation, and relativistic Lorentz factor. Our analysis shows that longitudinal two-stream modes dominate at small perpendicular wavenumbers and moderate drift velocities, while transverse Weibel modes become prevalent at high perpendicular wavenumbers and large velocity spreads or temperature anisotropies. These findings have direct implications for understanding magnetic field generation, particle acceleration, and energy dissipation in astrophysical pair plasmas including pulsar wind nebulae, gamma-ray burst internal shocks, and active galactic nuclei jets where counterstreaming pair populations naturally arise.

titles.title: Suppression of two-stream and Weibel instabilities in ultra-relativistic electron–positron plasma

abstracts.value: Realistic quantum devices are open systems, and their behaviour depends not only on the subsystem of interest but also on how the environment is modelled and how the relevant observables are extracted. This thesis studies that problem in three settings. First, we study cavity-assisted qubit readout beyond the dispersive regime. We show that once coherent excitation exchange and dissipation become relevant, a microscopic treatment is needed to describe the readout quantitatively, and the optimal readout is set by a trade-off between signal accumulation and the distinguishability of the readout states. Second, we compare fermionic and spin baths in non-interacting transport models and show that spin baths reproduce fermionic reduced dynamics only in the large-bath weak-coupling limit, while clear deviations appear for smaller baths and near half-filling. Third, we study charge transport in molecular junctions using Automated Compression of Environments (ACE). There, the main difficulty is not the time evolution itself, but the extraction of the transport current, since this observable depends on system-environment correlations and is therefore not contained in the reduced system density matrix alone. We show that a probe-mode construction provides a viable route to reformulate the current as a system observable. This thesis advances our understanding of what is required for accurate modelling of open quantum dynamics across a range of solid-state settings, from cavity-assisted qubit readout to charge transport in molecular junctions.

titles.title: Developing and validating models of open quantum systems in solid-state nanostructures

abstracts.value: Using superconducting rectifiers to energize high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets is a promising approach to accelerate the uptake of HTS magnet technology. In this work, we start to address two limitations of the HTS superconducting rectifier concepts published to date; their low magnet charging voltages, and the variable properties of their HTS-based switches. Our approach is to test a centre-tapped full-wave transformer–rectifier utilizing HTS secondary windings and switch-arrays of Si <sc xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mosfet</small>s mounted on a printed-circuit board (PCB). This approach has the advantage of greatly facilitating reproducible and reliable manufacture. The rectifier demonstrated magnet charging voltages exceeding a cycle-averaged 80 mV at 100 A and with typically more than 30% of the power supplied to the primary coils delivered to the magnet. We found it to be resilient to our preliminary thermal-cycling testing, with no degradation in performance observed over eight liquid-nitrogen to ambient (77–295 K) thermal cycles. We compare the impact of voltage- and current-controlled modes for the rectifier’s power supply. Our conclusion is that superconducting rectifiers using <sc xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mosfet</small> switch arrays placed on PCBs is a very promising approach for low-current HTS magnet power supplies.

titles.title: Using Printed Circuit Boards and MOSFET Switch Arrays Toward the Reliable Manufacture of Superconducting Rectifiers

abstracts.value: Compact high turns ratio superconducting transformers are used to transfer power between low-current copper/ semiconductor-based circuits and high-current superconductor-based circuits. This type of transformer is a key component in devices, such as superconducting transformer rectifiers and superconducting current source inverters. Typically the copper winding and the superconducting winding are arranged with a turn ratio above 100:1, respectively, and are situated entirely within a cryogenic environment. The ohmic losses associated with the high count copper winding is problematic for most cryogenic applications and demands attention even when low currents on the order of 1–10 A are used. To address this problem, a transformer has been made using rare-earth barium copper oxide (REBCO) high-temperature superconductor (HTS) coated conductor for both the primary and secondary windings. The coupling coefficient and power consumption of this transformer were measured and compared to an equivalent transformer consisting of a copper primary winding and HTS secondary winding. The HTS primary was found to provide a significant reduction in transformer power consumption and a slight improvement to transformer coupling at frequencies below <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim$</tex-math></inline-formula>8 Hz. An increased transformer core loss and winding AC loss began to negate these efficiency improvements above <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim$</tex-math></inline-formula>8 Hz. In addition, cowinding the primary and secondary windings provided a higher coupling coefficient and lower power consumption for all winding combinations and frequencies tested. Finally, a short discussion on the implications of these findings respect to superconducting transformer rectifiers contextualizes the findings.

titles.title: Compact High Turns Ratio Superconducting Transformer: Comparison Between Cu and REBCO Winding Materials

abstracts.value: This article investigates the mechanical characteristics and critical current performance of aluminum-stabilized stacked REBCO tape cable (ASTC) for the circular electron-positron collider detector magnet. In-plane bending, torsion, and uniaxial tension tests are carried out, combined by finite element analysis. The correlation between critical current and strain under different loading conditions is systematically analyzed, and key mechanical thresholds are determined. Results show that the minimum allowable in-plane bending diameter is 1200 mm. The critical twist pitch is 327 mm. The critical current degrades to 95% of the initial value when the tensile strain in the REBCO tape reaches 0.37%. This study provides essential experimental data and theoretical support for the structural design and engineering application of ASTC in high-field superconducting magnets.

titles.title: Mechanical Characteristics of Aluminium-Stabilized Stacked REBCO Tape Cable for the CEPC Detector Magnet

Introduction
One of the central challenges in string theory is to determine whether it admits phe-nomenologically viable four-dimensional vacua. A realistic compactification should re-produce, at sufficiently low energies, the essential features of observed particle physics.A widely studied possibility is that the resulting four-dimensional theory contains an
N = 1 supersymmetric matter sector, with supersymmetry spontaneously broken atan energy scale compatible with phenomenological constraints. The properties of thefour-dimensional effective theory are determined by the vacuum configuration of thecompactification. In particular, quantities such as gauge couplings, Yukawa couplings,particle masses, and supersymmetry-breaking parameters depend on the vacuum ex-pectation values of scalar fields known as moduli. These fields parametrise continuousdeformations of the internal geometry, as well as other background data characterisingthe compactification.

For a long time, the presence of unstabilised moduli represented one of the mainobstacles to connecting string theory with low-energy phenomenology. Massless mod-uli would mediate long-range fifth forces and, since their vacuum expectation valuesenter directly into physical observables, would prevent the theory from making definitepredictions. Although perturbative and non-perturbative quantum effects are generi-cally expected to generate a potential for the moduli in four-dimensional N = 1 the-ories, a systematic and parametrically controlled mechanism for stabilising all of themremained unavailable for many years.

A major advance was provided by the development of flux compactifications and bythe systematic study of their role in moduli stabilisation [7–9]. Type IIB string compact-ifications provide a particularly suitable setting for this programme. In this framework,background three-form fluxes generate a superpotential for the axio-dilaton S and thecomplex-structure moduli za, allowing these fields to be stabilised at tree level. TheKähler moduli Tα, by contrast, remain unfixed at this order as a consequence of the no-scale structure of the tree-level effective theory. Their stabilisation therefore requireseffects that are absent at the classical level. In particular, the interplay between non-perturbative contributions to the superpotential [10] and perturbativeα′ corrections tothe Kähler potential [11,12] generates a non-trivial scalar potential for the Kähler sector.This potential can be analysed within a controlled expansion at large internal volumeand leads to the Large Volume Scenario [1], in which the overall volume of the compact-ification is stabilised at an exponentially large value. Such vacua provide a particularlyrich framework for studying supersymmetry breaking and its possible phenomenologi-
1



cal consequences.

The resulting hierarchy naturally suggests a two-step treatment of moduli stabili-sation. One first determines the supersymmetric tree-level vacuum of the axio-dilatonand complex-structure sector by imposing the supersymmetric condition, and subse-quently, treats the fields (S, za) as effectively frozen while analysing the subleadingdynamics responsible for the stabilisation of the Kähler moduli. This procedure cap-tures the leading structure of the vacuum and forms the basis of the conventional four-dimensional LVS effective theory. However, the separation between the two sectors isnot exact. The perturbative and non-perturbative effects responsible for Kähler-modulistabilisation depend, in general, on the axio-dilaton and complex-structure moduli. Oncethese contributions are included, the complete scalar potential develops non-vanishinggradients along the (S, za) directions. Consequently, the original tree-level flux vac-uum is displaced from its supersymmetric position [2,6]. The assumption that the flux-stabilised fields remain exactly frozen therefore neglects their backreaction on the fullvacuum.

The purpose of this thesis is to investigate this effect systematically. In particular, wedetermine explicitly the displacement of the axio-dilaton and complex-structure vac-uum induced by the subleading corrections responsible for Kähler-moduli stabilisation.The corrected minimum is computed perturbatively around the tree-level flux vacuum,organising the analysis according to the parametric dependence on the compactifica-tion volume V and the string coupling gs. Our results are derived in the controlledregime of exponentially large volume and weak string coupling,
V ≫ 1, gs ≪ 1. (0.1)

This allows us to identify the leading contributions to the vacuum shifts and to de-termine their scaling in the simultaneous large-volume and weak-coupling expansions.Once the corrected vacuum configuration has been determined, one can compute thecorrespondingF -terms, which provide the relevant order parameters for supersymme-try breaking in the four-dimensional effective theory.

A central result of this analysis is that the contribution induced by the displacementof the vacuum is not parametrically negligible. For the axio-dilaton, the shift-inducedcorrection enters at the same order in the simultaneous expansions in gs and V−1 asthe contribution obtained by evaluating the corrected F -terms at the unshifted tree-level vacuum. In the complex-structure direction, the effect is even more pronounced:
2



the shift-induced contribution is enhanced by an additional factor of g−1
s relative tothe corresponding unshifted term. Therefore, despite the smallness of the vacuum dis-placement itself, its effect on the F -terms can be of leading-order relevance, in theweak-coupling regime.We first study this mechanism in a simplified model with a rigid complex-structuresector, in which only the axio-dilaton S is displaced. We then extend the analysis toa model containing a dynamical complex-structure modulus and explicitly account forthe mixing between the S and z directions. This allows us to determine both the para-metric behaviour and the explicit form of the shifts δS and δz in the large-volume andweak-coupling expansions.

As previously stated, the corrections to the axio-dilaton and complex-structure F -terms can have direct phenomenological consequences. In sequestered LVS scenarios,soft supersymmetry-breaking terms depend sensitively on the auxiliary fields of theflux-stabilized sector [3]. We find that the shift of the vacuum does not parametricallymodify F S , so that soft terms whose leading contribution is controlled by the axio-dilaton auxiliary field retain the standard LVS scaling. By contrast, the modified complex-structure F -terms can give parametrically different contributions to observables whichdepend directly on F z, including scalar masses in the ultra-local regime.A further application concerns the supersymmetric partners of closed-string hiddenphotons. In type IIB orientifold compactifications, RR photons arise from the dimen-sional reduction of the RR four-form C(4) on orientifold-even three-cycles, and theirgauge kinetic functions are controlled by the complex-structure moduli [4, 13]. Con-sequently, the corresponding hidden-photino masses depend directly on the complex-structure F -terms. Therefore, any parametric modification of F za induced by the dis-placement of the flux vacuum is directly inherited by the hidden-photino mass, up tothe model-dependent complex-structure dependence of the gauge kinetic function.These examples provide a direct connection between the corrections studied in thiswork and the low-energy phenomenology of sequestered string compactifications.

This thesis is organised as follows. The first two chapters provide the theoreticalbackground required for the subsequent analysis. After reviewing the essential ele-ments of four-dimensional supergravity, we introduce the main features of superstringtheory and of Type IIB compactifications. Particular attention is devoted to the fieldcontent and effective description of Type IIB orientifolds with O3/O7-planes, with theaim of defining the quantities and conventions needed throughout the rest of the the-sis. Chapter 3 is devoted to the problem of moduli stabilisation. We first discuss the roleof background fluxes in fixing the axio-dilaton and complex-structure moduli and thenintroduce the Large Volume Scenario as a mechanism for stabilising the Kähler sector.

3



In this context, we emphasise the conventional two-step procedure in which the fluxsector is stabilised at tree level and subsequently treated as effectively frozen whenanalysing the subleading Kähler-moduli dynamics. The final chapter contains the orig-inal results of this work. We compute explicitly the displacement of the flux-stabilisedvacuum induced by the perturbative and non-perturbative corrections responsible forLVS stabilisation. The analysis is first carried out in a simplified toy model with rigidcomplex structure and is then extended to a more general setting including a dynamicalcomplex-structure modulus. We finally determine the corresponding corrections to theaxio-dilaton and complex-structure F -terms and analyse their parametric behaviour inthe large-volume and weak-coupling regime.

1 Supersymmetry and Supergravity
Supersymmetry is a spacetime symmetry relating bosonic and fermionic degrees offreedom and organizing them into common supermultiplets. It plays a fundamentalrole in superstring theory, whose development was historically motivated by the at-tempt to incorporate fermionic excitations into the bosonic string.The low-energy dynamics of string compactifications is naturally described in termsof supersymmetric field theories. In four-dimensional compactifications preserving foursupercharges, the relevant framework is N = 1 supersymmetry. We therefore beginthis chapter by reviewing the basic structure of four-dimensional rigid supersymmetry,introducing its algebra, the corresponding supermultiplets, and the supersymmetric ac-tions.We then turn to local supersymmetry, obtained by promoting the parameters of su-persymmetry transformations to spacetime-dependent spinors. Such a local symmetrycannot be consistently realized without introducing gravity: the corresponding gaugetheory necessarily contains the graviton, together with its fermionic superpartner, thegravitino. The resulting framework is N = 1, D = 4 supergravity.Finally, we present the supergravity action for chiral and vector multiplets coupledto gravity, emphasizing the role of the Kähler potential, the superpotential, and thegauge kinetic functions. Particular attention will be devoted to the scalar potential andto the auxiliary F -terms, which provide the essential language for describing modulistabilization and supersymmetry breaking in four-dimensional effective theories arisingfrom string compactifications.

1.4 Supersymmetry breaking
If supersymmetry is realized in Nature, it cannot be an exact symmetry at the energyscales currently accessible to experiments. Indeed, exact supersymmetry would requirethe bosonic and fermionic states belonging to the same supermultiplet to have identicalmasses. No such mass degeneracy has been observed in the spectrum of elementaryparticles.Supersymmetry must therefore be broken at some characteristic scale, which wedenote by MSUSY. At energies much larger than this scale, the effects responsiblefor the breaking may become negligible, and the theory approaches its supersymmet-ric limit. This statement is particularly natural when supersymmetry is broken by softterms.There are two conceptually distinct ways in which supersymmetry may be broken:

• Spontaneous supersymmetry breaking. The Lagrangian is exactly supersymmet-ric, but the vacuum is not invariant under the action of the supercharges. In aglobally supersymmetric theory, this occurs when at least one auxiliary field ac-quires a non-vanishing vacuum expectation value.
• Explicit supersymmetry breaking. The Lagrangian contains terms which are not in-variant under supersymmetry transformations. A generic explicit breaking wouldspoil the ultraviolet cancellations which motivate supersymmetry. One thereforeusually restricts to soft supersymmetry-breaking terms, which do not reintroducequadratic ultraviolet divergences. Their coefficients have positive mass dimen-sion, so their effects become progressively less important at energies much largerthan the supersymmetry-breaking scale.
Typical soft-breaking operators include scalar mass terms, gaugino masses and scalartrilinear and bilinear interactions. Although these terms explicitly break supersymme-try, they preserve the improved ultraviolet behaviour of the supersymmetric theory.

2 Superstrings
In this chapter, we review the main ingredients of type II superstring theory that arerequired for the compactification framework developed in the remainder of this thesis[15]. We begin with the Ramond–Neveu–Schwarz formulation of superstrings in ten-dimensional flat Minkowski spacetime, emphasizing the role of worldsheet fermions,the Neveu–Schwarz and Ramond sectors, and the GSO projection. The latter removesthe tachyonic state and leads to a spectrum containing both spacetime bosons andfermions, organized into supersymmetric multiplets.Among the five consistent superstring theories in ten dimensions, type IIA, type IIB,type I, and the two heterotic theories with gauge groups SO(32) and E8 × E8, wefocus on the type II theories, and in particular on type IIB string theory, which providesthe ten-dimensional starting point for the compactifications considered in this work.We therefore review it massless spectra and its corresponding low-energy supergravitydescriptions.We then turn to compactifications on Calabi–Yau threefolds. After introducing thegeometric and cohomological properties of Calabi–Yau manifolds, we discuss how theten-dimensional massless fields give rise to four-dimensional fields through Kaluza–Klein reduction. Compactification of type II string theory on a Calabi–Yau threefold pre-servesN = 2 supersymmetry in four dimensions. To obtain theN = 1 effective theoryrelevant for moduli stabilization, we subsequently introduce orientifold projections andspecialize to type IIB Calabi–Yau orientifolds withO3/O7-planes. This construction de-termines the surviving moduli fields and their organization into four-dimensional chiraland vector multiplets, providing the setting in which fluxes, the effective Kähler poten-tial, and the corrections to the moduli F -terms will be studied.

2.3 Type II Compactifications
We now discuss how the ten-dimensional supergravity theories arising as the low-energylimits of type II string theories can be reduced to four dimensions. In the simplest classof compactifications, one considers an unwarped product geometry of the form

M10 =M4 ×X6, (2.47)

At this stage, we assume that the dilaton is constant and that all back-ground form-field strengths vanish, so that the only non-trivial background field is theten-dimensional metric.If the compactification is required to preserve part of the ten-dimensional super-symmetry, the geometry of X6 is strongly constrained. Compactification of either typeIIA or type IIB supergravity on a Calabi–Yau threefold with holonomy exactlySU(3) pre-serves eight real supercharges and therefore gives an N = 2 supersymmetric theoryin four dimensions. Additional ingredients, such as orientifold projections, are requiredto reduce the supersymmetry further to N = 1.

2.4 Type II orientifolds
Orientifold projections of Type II Calabi–Yau compactifications provide a standard mech-anism for reducing four-dimensional supersymmetry from N = 2 to N = 1. They in-troduce orientifold planes and require the inclusion of D-branes for Ramond–Ramondcharge cancellation, thereby also giving rise to gauge sectors and charged matter in thefour-dimensional effective theory.Starting from Type II string theory compactified on a Calabi–Yau threefold X3, onequotients the theory by a discrete orientifold action involving worldsheet parity and aninvolution of the internal manifold. Depending on the Type II theory and on the classof orientifold, the orientifold operator takes the form

O = (−1)FLΩσ. (2.83)
Here Ω reverses the orientation of the string worldsheet, FL is the spacetime fermionnumber in the left-moving sector, and σ is an involutive isometry of the internal Calabi–Yau manifold,

σ2 = id. (2.84)
The precise form of O, as well as the action of σ on the Calabi–Yau geometry, dependson the orientifold construction under consideration.The geometric fixed loci of σ support orientifold planes. An Op-plane extends alongthe four non-compact spacetime dimensions and wraps an internal cycle of real dimen-sion p−3. In the standard orientifold constructions considered here, these objects carrynegative Ramond–Ramond charge and negative tension. Their total Ramond–Ramondcharge must be cancelled by appropriate configurations of D-branes and, when rele-vant, background fluxes. This requirement is encoded in the corresponding Ramond–Ramond tadpole-cancellation conditions.Spacetime-filling D-branes extend along the four non-compact dimensions and wrapinternal cycles of X3. They need not wrap the same cycles as the orientifold planes.Rather, the total charge carried by the D-branes and their orientifold images must can-cel the charges of the orientifold planes, together with any flux-induced contributions,in the appropriate homology or cohomology class. Open strings ending on the D-branesgive rise to four-dimensional gauge fields and charged matter multiplets.Preservation of four-dimensional N = 1 supersymmetry imposes further condi-tions on the involution σ. In Type IIB orientifolds, σ acts holomorphically on the Calabi–Yau manifold, whereas in the standard Type IIA constructions it acts antiholomorphi-cally. Its action assigns definite parities to the Kähler form J , the holomorphic three-form Ω, and the ten-dimensional form fields. The orientifold projection retains onlythe degrees of freedom invariant under the combined action O, thereby truncating theoriginal four-dimensional N = 2 spectrum to an N = 1 spectrum.

3 Large Volume Scenario
The four-dimensional massless spectrum arising from string compactifications gener-ally contains a large number of scalar fields, known as moduli. In Type IIB Calabi–Yauorientifold compactifications with O3/O7-planes, whose field content is summarized inTable 2, these fields parametrise continuous deformations of the internal geometry anddetermine several effective four-dimensional couplings. If they remain unstabilized, themoduli correspond to flat directions of the scalar potential and may give rise to lightscalar degrees of freedom. Such fields can mediate long-range interactions and inducephenomenological effects that are incompatible with current observations. A realisticstring compactification must therefore provide a mechanism that lifts these flat direc-tions, fixes the vacuum expectation values of the moduli, and generates sufficientlylarge masses for them.In this chapter, we review the Large Volume Scenario (LVS), which provides a sys-tematic framework for moduli stabilization in Type IIB flux compactifications. The sta-bilization mechanism proceeds hierarchically. At leading order, background three-formfluxes stabilize the axio-dilaton and the complex-structure moduli at a supersymmetricminimum, while the Kähler moduli remain unfixed as a consequence of the no-scalestructure. Their stabilization is subsequently achieved by including perturbative α′ cor-rections to the Kähler potential together with non-perturbative contributions to the su-perpotential. This two-step structure will play a central role in the analysis developedin the remainder of this thesis.

5 Conclusions and Outlook
The Large Volume Scenario is commonly analysed through a two-step procedure. Attree level, background fluxes stabilise the axio-dilaton and the complex-structure mod-uli at a supersymmetric vacuum, while the Kähler moduli remain unfixed because ofthe no-scale structure. Perturbative and non-perturbative effects are then included tostabilise the Kähler sector, treating the flux-stabilised fields as effectively frozen at theirtree-level values.This separation provides a controlled description of the vacuum at leading orderin the inverse-volume expansion. It is, however, not exact. The effects responsible forKähler-moduli stabilisation depend in general on the axio-dilaton and complex-structuremoduli and therefore generate non-vanishing gradients along these directions. As aconsequence, the tree-level flux vacuum is displaced once the complete scalar poten-tial is taken into account.The purpose of this thesis has been to study this displacement systematically andto determine how it modifies the auxiliary fields associated with the flux-stabilised sec-tor. Particular attention has been devoted to the simultaneous large-volume and weak-coupling expansions,

V ≫ 1, gs ≪ 1, (5.1)
which provide the parametric control required by the four-dimensional effective de-scription.The corrected vacuum was determined perturbatively by separating the scalar po-tential into its leading flux contribution and the subleading terms. This procedure makesexplicit that the magnitude of the displacement is determined not only by the correct-ing potential, but also by the inverse Hessian of the tree-level flux vacuum. The lattercarries a non-trivial dependence on the string coupling and plays an essential role inthe final power counting.In the first simplified model, the only displaced flux-stabilised field is the axio-dilaton.The calculation showed that the shift of S generates an additional contribution to itsauxiliary field F S . This contribution scales parametrically as

Nevertheless, itcontributes to the numerical coefficient ofF S at the first non-vanishing order and mustconsequently be included in a complete computation at this accuracy.

Analysis of the harmonic flow

of geometric structures

Eric Loubeau
Département de Mathématiques
LMBA / UMR 6205
Université de Bretagne Occidentale
6, avenue Victor Le Gorgeu
CS 93837, 29238 Brest Cedex 3, France
eric.loubeau@univ-brest.fr

Received: March 5, 2025; accepted: June 10, 2025.

Abstract. We develop an analysis of the flow of harmonic H-structures with the strategy
introduced by Chen-Struwe for the harmonic map heat equation when the target does not
necessarily have negative sectional curvature, so the Eells-Sampson Theorem cannot apply.

In particular, this flow method enables us to find theoretical hypotheses under which the
existence of a torsion-free H-structure is guaranteed and conditions for which the flow must
blow up in finite time.

This extends results already known for some specific groups like U(n), G2 or Spin(7).

Keywords: Geometric structures; harmonic maps; harmonic sections, heat flow

MSC 2020 classification: primary 53C10, 53C15, 53C43, 58E20, 53E30

1 Holonomy and geometric structures

Berger’s 1955 theorem gives the list of the seven possible holonomy groups
of an irreducible, non-symmetric, simply-connected Riemannian n-dimensional
manifold: SO(n) (the general case), U(n2 ) (Kähler), SU(n2 ) (Calabi-Yau), Sp(n4 )
(Hyper-Kähler), Sp(n4 )Sp(1) (Quaternionic-Kähler), G2 (n = 7), Spin(7) (n =
8); plus the group Spin(9) for n = 16, before it was removed by Alekseevskij [1].

Moreover, each case is characterised by the existence of a parallel (multi-)
tensor, with respect to the Levi-Civita connection of (M, g).

For SO(n), it is the unobstructed condition of a torsion-free connection,
the Kähler case is equivalent to the existence of a parallel almost Hermitian
structure, etc.

For G2, the parallel three-form ϕ must, point-wise, be given in some frame
of TpM by

ϕp = e123 − e1 ∧ (e45 − e67) + e2 ∧ (e46 − e57) + e3 ∧ (e47 − e56),

130 E. Loubeau

while for Spin(7), Φ ∈ Λ4(T ∗M) and the local model is

Φp = e0123 − e0145 − e0167 − e0246 + e0257 − e0347 − e0356

+ e4567 − e2367 − e2345 − e1357 + e1346 − e1256 − e1247

where

e0123 = dx0 ∧ dx1 ∧ dx2 ∧ dx3.

The significance of holonomy is twofold. First, it informs on the curvature tensor
as it must live in the holonomy Lie algebra and this implies for SU(n2 ), Sp(n4 ),
G2 and Spin(7) that the manifold is Ricci-flat.

On the other hand, manifolds with special holonomy are the cornerstone
of higher-dimensional Gauge Theory. For example, take n = 7 and G2, then
a vector bundle E → M7 with connection ∇ has curvature F∇ ∈ Λ2, so the
condition ∗F∇ = λF∇ (λ ∈ R) does not make sense anymore and we must
introduce a three-form to counterbalance the degrees. If chosen closed, it will
allow for Yang-Mills connections.

The disadvantage is that it is generally hard to construct manifolds with spe-
cial holonomy, as the problem is highly non-linear, especially when the defining
tensor determines the metric. For example, local solutions of G2-manifolds first
appear in 1984 [3], complete ones in 1986 [4] and compact constructions only as
late as 1996-2000 with Joyce [15, 16].

An alternative, softer and more topological in nature, is to consider H-
structures (H ⊂ SO(n)), which are reductions of the structure group and can
also be seen as sections of an ad-hoc twistor space constructed as the H-quotient
of the unitary frame bundle PSO(n).

Locally, H-structures are described by (multi-) tensors given at each point
by a Euclidean prototype and stabilized by the group H.

It relies on a model (p, q)-tensor ξ0 ∈ T p,q(Rn) on the Euclidean space,
stabilised by the group H = Stab(ξ0) = {g ∈ GL(n,R) : g.ξ0 = ξ0} under the
GL(n,R) right action

g.ξ0 = ξ
i1...ip

On the manifold (M, g), an H-structure ξ is a (multi-) tensor such that at
any point p ∈ M there is a frame of TpM that identifies ξp and ξ0 (or several
ξ0’s in case of a multi-tensor).

In fact, this approach goes further than Berger’s list and includes new cases
such as almost contact structures (H = U(n)× Id ⊂ SO(2n + 1)), parallelisms
(i.e. global orthonormal frames for H = {1}) or unit vector fields (H = SO(n−
1) ⊂ SO(n)) and others of varying degrees of interest.



Harmonic geometric structures 131

Finally, one should add that H-structures with torsion, i.e. non-parallel, are
key ingredients in several theories of Mathematical Physics, for example the
models of Supersymmetric AdS4 compactifications of IIA supergravity of Lüst
and Tsimpis [19]. This fact alone should be sufficient reason for their study.

2 Harmonic maps and harmonicity

For an abstract (smooth) map φ from a compact Riemannian manifold
(M, g) to (N,h), the Dirichlet energy is

E(φ) =

where the energy density 1

∗h. Critical points of E are

called harmonic maps [10] and the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equation is
the vanishing of the tension field

τ(φ) = trace∇dφ.

The energy functional is conformally invariant when dimM = 2 and harmonic
maps generalise harmonic functions (N = R), geodesics (dimM = 1), totally
geodesic maps (since ∇dφ = 0), minimal submanifolds (isometric immersions)
and holomorphic maps between Kähler manifolds. Cf. [2, Chap. 3] for details
and examples.

The groundbreaking work of Eells and Sampson [10] did not just introduced
this notion but also proved the existence of a harmonic representative in each
homotopy class when the target has non-positive sectional curvature. One should
however keep in mind that if there only exists a single homotopy class, it will
contain the trivially-harmonic constant maps.

Perhaps, as important was the heat-flow method they employed which has
known a rich legacy, all the way to Hamilton’s Ricci flow and Perelman’s proof
of the Poincaré conjecture.

This method is perhaps just as compelling by its failure when the curvature
condition on the target is not met and the flow develops bubbles and explodes,
as is the case of the sphere S2 to itself. This was superbly exploited by Sachs
and Uhlenbeck with a reparametrization process enabling to restart the flow
and accounting for the topological penalties in terms of energy quantization.

Paradoxically, for the two-sphere, these pitfalls of the heat flow can eas-
ily be circumvented by considering holomorphic maps and produce harmonic
representatives in each and every homotopy class.

The best-known situation where harmonic maps do not exist is for degree-
one maps from the two-torus to the two-sphere [11]. Indeed, such a map would



132 E. Loubeau

have to be conformal, hence holomorphic, which is forbidden for degree one by
Riemann-Roch.

In higher dimensions, one of the most often encountered example is the Hopf
map from S3 to S2 and, as a Riemannian submersion with minimal fibres, it also
happens to be a harmonic morphism.

In spite of decades of work on harmonic maps, relatively little has been done
for sections, except perhaps for vector fields [7], and C. M. Wood was the first to
consider almost Hermitian structures as sections of the twistor space and study
them under the light of harmonicity [20].

The point here is not merely to compute the tension field of a particular
map but more precisely to consider the Dirichlet energy of sections and search
for its critical points among sections, in order to compare like with like.

On a philosophical level, there is no reason to limit this to the specific case
of almost Hermitian structures and any type of reduction of structures on a
Riemannian manifold can be the subjected to the same treatment.

3 The Heat flow

The ultimate objective of the heat flow of geometric structures is to pro-
vide conditions ensuring the existence of an absolute minimiser of the Dirichlet
energy and answer the question of torsion-free geometric structures in a given
homotopy class.

With a target of positive curvature, one cannot hope to apply Eells-Sampson’s
original proof and must turn to Chen-Struwe’s arguments. In the end, this ap-
proach leads to a threshold for the Dirichlet energy of the initial data under
which convergence will happen to a torsion-free solution. By contraposition,
this lower bound can also be used to obtain singularity results.

This method is based on a series of more or less technical results but first,
one should recall that short-time existence is an automatic consequence of the
harmonic map equation. The main equation we will work with is the Bochner
formula which essentially turns the heat flow equation, living in the pull-back
of the vertical space of the twistor space, i.e. the bundle associated with the
isotropic representation, into a scalar expression at the cost of becoming an
inequality.

The Shi-type estimates control, along the flow, the norms of the derivatives
of the torsion (basically the coderivatives of the geometric structure) in terms
of the torsion itself and the derivatives of the curvature.

Both these results are valid for a general group H ⊂ SO(n) (and even more
cf. [9]).

The cornerstone of the whole strategy is the Almost Monotonicity Formula
(AMF) for a time-dependent functional which integrates, over a geodesic ball,
the product of the energy density and the backward heat kernel with singularity
at the centre of the ball (along with localisation by a cut-off function).



138 E. Loubeau

This AMF will prompt the ε-regularity of the heat flow which draws a point-
wise bound of the energy density from a bound on the integral of the function
involved in the AMF.

This opens the gates, not only for energy gap results but also for long-time
existence and finite-time singularity statements.

Indeed, by a refined treatment of the Bochner formula, due to Chen-Ding
[5], controlling the existence interval of the harmonic flow, one can prove that
if the energy density remains bounded over the maximal existence interval then
the flow exists for all time and converges to a harmonic solution.

On the other hand, if it explodes then the maximal existence-time must be
less than (the square-root of) the initial energy.

To conclude, bounds on the Dirichlet energy and L∞-norm of the initial data
exclude explosion of the energy density over the maximal existence interval,
hence force long-time existence and convergence toward a torsion-free solution.

Additionally, if no torsion-free H-structure exists in a given homotopy class
while the infimum of the Dirichlet energy is indeed zero, small enough initial
Dirichlet energy will make the flow develop a finite-time singularity.

Versions of these results for specific groups H can be found in [14, 8] but
note that groups like SU(n) are not covered by these results.

abstracts.value: Recently, influence of strong fields on nuclear decay processes is progressively becoming a topic of great interest plus the existence of some ambiguities. In this study, an approximate calculation of the Schrödinger equation with reduced <math><mi>r</mi></math> dependence is employed instead of the classical Coulomb wave-function program to provide a description of decay width and decay energy in quasistatic (adiabatic) laser fields. More importantly, going beyond the quasistatic approximation, the strict time evolution of the wave function and the periodic modulation of the decay energy are investigated by solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation with the split operator method, which captures the dynamical behavior of the <math><mi>α</mi></math> cluster during the decay process. First, our results corroborate earlier reports that the decay width is modified only negligibly by strong laser fields. Likewise, the shift in decay energy is found to be extremely small, which validates the rationality of using fixed experimental decay energies in earlier studies. This modification effect will exist more obviously in a nucleus with the higher proton-neutron asymmetry, the lower decay energy, and the octupole deformation. Second, our results demonstrate that strong fields can indeed produce a periodic modulation of decay energy, with a cycle mean shift on the order of <math><mrow><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup><mspace width="4pt"/><mi>eV</mi></mrow></math> at an intensity of <math><mrow><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>24</mn></msup><mspace width="4pt"/><mi mathvariant="normal">W</mi><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>cm</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>.

abstracts.value: Spin squeezing is a genuine multipartite entanglement resource enabling quantum-enhanced metrology beyond classical limits. Based on a hybrid solid-state system of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers and magnons, we propose a scheme for generating spin squeezing via Kerr nonlinearity. In the large-detuning regime, by tuning the strength of the magnon parametric amplification (MPA) enabled by Kerr effect, the magnon-mediated spin-spin interactions can be controlled, thereby allowing flexible switching among one-axis twisting (OAT), two-axis twisting (TAT), and unconventional two-axis twisting (UTAT). Remarkably, in the presence of realistic dissipation and finite-size effects, an optimized UTAT interaction exhibits enhanced spin squeezing and quantum-enhanced sensing performance compared with the corresponding OAT and TAT cases. Furthermore, in the resonant and strongly dissipative regime, the MPA-induced TAT interaction and squeezed magnon reservoir jointly enable steady-state spin squeezing of the NV ensemble. Our results establish a unified and flexible scheme for generating both dynamical and steady-state spin squeezing, with potential applications in quantum-enhanced precision measurements.

titles.title: Dynamical and stable spin squeezing via magnon Kerr nonlinearity in a hybrid solid-state system

abstracts.value: We design an atom-waveguide system to achieve nonreciprocal frequency conversion. Single-photon frequency conversion is achieved through inelastic scattering mediated by the V-type giant atom with one transition coupled to a one-dimensional coupled-resonator waveguide (CRW) and the other transition coherently driven by a classical field. To quantitatively characterize the frequency-conversion efficiency, we define scattering flows by incorporating the corresponding group velocities. The reciprocity and nonreciprocity of the system can be characterized by the conversion-flow contrast. It is found that the single-photon frequency-conversion flow is closely related to the size of the giant atom and the phase difference between the coupling strengths at the two atom-CRW coupling sites. Under reciprocal conditions, the maximum conversion flow is strictly bounded by <math><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, regardless of how the giant atom size and the phase difference are tuned. When reciprocity is broken, tuning the coupling phase at a fixed giant atom size significantly enhances the maximum conversion flow, which can even reach unity. Meanwhile, the conversion-flow contrast reaches its extremal values, corresponding to perfect single-photon nonreciprocity.

titles.title: Nonreciprocal frequency conversion of single photons in a one-dimensional coupled-resonator waveguide

abstracts.value: The development of large-scale superconducting quantum computers critically depends on the accurate readout of qubit states. To enable this, cryogenic parametric amplifiers have been proposed and developed, and have since found widespread use in small-signal detection applications. Among various amplifier architectures, Josephson traveling-wave parametric amplifiers (JTWPAs) are widely adopted due to their broad bandwidth, high saturation power, and compatibility with superconducting qubits. In this work, we present a design workflow of JTWPAs based on a cosimulation approach combining electromagnetic (EM) and circuit-level simulation. We apply this method to a uniform JTWPA, comparing our simulation results with experimental data. To mitigate the challenge of constructing lumped-element circuit models usually used in the conventional simulation method, we directly perform full EM analysis of the device to accurately determine its linear response. The extracted S-parameters are then fed into a nonlinear harmonic balance simulator with Josephson junctions modeled as circuit elements. By doing so, the linear and gain properties of the JTWPA are extracted. Different factors that impact device performance including gain compression, phase matching, and fabrication imperfections are further investigated and modeled. A good agreement between simulation and measurements is identified, establishing the effectiveness of our approach in designing quantum parametric amplifiers.

titles.title: Designing Josephson Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifiers: EM-Circuit Cosimulation and Experimental Validation

abstracts.value: Quantum computing (QC) emulation is critical for exploring and advancing near-term quantum algorithms, given the ongoing scalability and reliability challenges of quantum hardware. While FPGA-based QC emulators have emerged as efficient alternatives to bridge the gap toward practical quantum computers, most existing solutions depend on high-performance systems, limiting their applicability in embedded and edge environments. In this work, we present a scalable, standalone FPGA-based emulator specialized for resource-constrained systems. Our design targets the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), particularly for the Weighted-MaxCut problem. By leveraging diagonal decomposition and a pipeline-centric hardware architecture, we reduce the computational complexity of QAOA from $\boldsymbol{O(N^{2})}$ to $\boldsymbol{O(N)}$, where $\boldsymbol{N}$ $\boldsymbol{=}$ $\boldsymbol{2^{n}}$ is the state dimension for $\boldsymbol{n}$ qubits. This reformulation and its architectural co-design significantly reduces hardware overhead, enabling larger qubit configurations on edge-level FPGAs. We encapsulate these optimizations into a hardware accelerator called the Quantum MaxCut Accelerator (QMA), which integrates seamlessly into a RISC-V platform, forming a self-contained emulator. Additionally, we introduce QC Emulator eXpress (QEX), a full-stack automation framework that streamlines QMA integration into configurable RISC-V platforms, significantly facilitating rapid and scalable emulator development and deployment. Through extensive prototyping of various QAOA emulators, our experiments confirm that the proposed QMA achieves energy reductions of up to $\textbf{907}\boldsymbol{\times}$ compared to the CPU-only software baseline under the same standalone FPGA/RISC-V setting and reliably supports up to 9 qubits on a mid-tier FPGA. These results demonstrate the energy efficiency and scalability of the proposed system as a self-contained FPGA/RISC-V platform for edge-local QAOA emulation, prototyping, and HW/SW co-design exploration under resource-constrained conditions.

titles.title: Quantum at the Edge: Scalable Standalone FPGA Emulator for QAOA-Based Weighted-MaxCut

abstracts.value: Solitons are fundamental entities in nonlinear wave equations across diverse branches of physics. In systems with competing nonlinearities, a hallmark transition occurs from traditional bell-shaped profiles to flat-top configurations as the norm increases. In this work, we analyze double flat-top solitons in systems of two coupled generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equations. We develop a theoretical and variational framework that provides both physical insight and a computationally efficient description of these eigenstates. In the large-norm regime, and for a broad class of nonlinear potentials supporting flat-top states, we derive explicit analytical expressions for the plateau densities and chemical potentials, together with variational estimates for the interfacial properties characterizing the solutions. These quantities are controlled by algebraic conditions that generalize the Maxwell coexistence condition to coupled wave functions. We show that two-component flat-top solitons may form core–shell configurations, in which a two-component core is surrounded by a shell of the dominant species, as well as no-shell configurations, where both species occupy the same spatial domain. Using the cubic-quintic nonlinearity as a prototypical model, we compare these analytical predictions with direct numerical computations of the stationary states and find excellent agreement in the flat-top regime. The resulting picture admits a natural interpretation in terms of phase coexistence in an effective binary fluid, with kink-like interfaces carrying an excess grand potential that plays the role of a surface tension. This formalism is applicable to diverse physical platforms, including nonlinear optics, multicomponent Bose–Einstein condensates, and Q-ball configurations in relativistic field theories.

titles.title: Theory of double flat-top solitons in coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equations

abstracts.value: Locally recoverable codes (LRCs) are classical error-correcting codes widely used in large-scale distributed and cloud storage systems. Quantum locally recoverable codes of locality <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$(r,\delta)$ </tex-math></inline-formula> (quantum <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$(r,\delta)$ </tex-math></inline-formula>-LRCs) are the quantum counterpart of classical <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$(r,\delta)$ </tex-math></inline-formula>-LRCs. They allow us to correct erasures at several positions using a trace-preserving quantum operation acting on qudits of a larger set of positions. We consider matrix-product codes (MPCs) <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\mathcal {C}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> and give constituent (or defining) matrices and conditions on the constituent codes such that the codes <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\mathcal {C}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> satisfy the conditions to provide quantum <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$(r,\delta)$ </tex-math></inline-formula>-LRCs. As a consequence, we are able to determine their locality and parameters. abstracts.value: Linear codes constructed from combinatorial and geometric structures have played a central role in both classical and quantum coding theory. In this paper, we discuss a class of linear codes over finite fields, called polytope codes, obtained via defining sets derived from lattice polytopes. Unlike evaluation-based constructions, our approach exploits the intersection structure of polytope faces to directly control the algebraic and metric properties of the resulting codes. We develop a general defining-set framework for polytope codes and explicitly determine their lengths, dimensions, minimum distances, and Hamming weight distributions. This leads to infinite families of projective, few-weight, distance-optimal, and almost distance-optimal codes. Sufficient conditions for minimality are derived, resulting in new minimal codes that are well suited for applications to secret-sharing schemes. We further study the duals and hulls of polytope codes and provide explicit characterizations of self-orthogonal and linear complementary dual (LCD) families. One of the central results of the paper is a complete classification of quantum codes arising from polytope codes via the Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) construction. We show that the geometry of face intersections fully determines whether the resulting quantum code is a standard CSS code, an LCD-based code, or an entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting code, and we explicitly compute the required entanglement in the latter case. As a consequence, new families of binary, ternary, and prime-power quantum codes with previously unattained parameters are obtained. The proposed polytope-based framework unifies classical and quantum code constructions under a common geometric principle and opens new avenues for applications in cryptography, distributed storage, and quantum information processing. abstracts.value: We present an example of a simple special relativity technique that professional high-energy particle physicists use in their searches for new particles. Modern particle detectors are designed to measure the momentum and energy of particles that result from proton-proton collisions. Researchers then use this kinematic information to identify properties of the short-lived heavy particles created during the proton–proton collisions. The most famous recent example is the measurement of the invariant mass of the Higgs Boson. One problem these researchers face is that not all particles created during the collisions are detectable. Neutrinos, sometimes called “ghost particles,” are essentially invisible to modern particle detectors, and therefore seemingly make it impossible to recover the complete information about the underlying collision. In this article, we will show how researchers use other information about the collisions to identify the momentum and energy of these invisible particles, and then use that information to search for new particles, including those predicted in supersymmetric models. This technique is simple enough for students in a modern physics course that covers special relativity and basic particle physics, yet powerful enough to aid physicists searching for the newest and highest energy particles.

abstracts.value: Blazar jets, originating very close to supermassive black holes, are modeled using special relativity, electricity, magnetism, and particle physics. Astronomers use the light emitted within blazar jets to understand the extremely energetic relativistic plasma that resides there. Students are often curious about these topics, and concrete examples of how they play out in nature can be helpful to motivate their learning of fundamental physics. Here, we give four examples of topics that are covered in a Modern Physics course, but they may also be interesting in the context of more advanced physics courses like Special Relativity and Particle Physics. First, we show how special relativity applies to large-scale blazar jets. Second, we show how synchrotron radiation within a highly collimated jet of tenuous plasma produces X-rays. These X-rays, originally discovered in quasar spectra, were the first hallmark of non-thermal acceleration. Third, we show how inverse-Compton scattering occurs and is observed as high-energy γ-rays by an astronomer. Finally, we show that pair production can occur when a high-energy γ-ray intercepts starlight on its way toward the astronomer and how the mean-free path of the γ-rays creates a TeV Cosmic Horizon. Example homework problems appropriate for a Modern Physics class are provided for instructors.

titles.title: Blazars: A laboratory for exploring modern physics

abstracts.value: We exactly solve the two-dimensional Dirac equation for a charged particle subject to a uniform magnetic field in the noncommutative Snyder-de Sitter space, whose algebra combines coordinate noncommutativity with a curvature of momentum space. Working in the momentum-space differential representation, and keeping a mixing parameter $\lambda $ free up to the spectral stage, we derive the associated second-order radial equation and then eliminate its first-derivative term to bring it to the form of an effective Schrödinger-type Hamiltonian. This Hamiltonian is factorized within the framework of supersymmetric quantum mechanics and is shown to be shape invariant under a simple translation of its parameters, which allows the energy spectrum and eigenstates to be obtained analytically. We show that the requirement of a real spectrum uniquely fixes the value of the parameter $\lambda $. The commutative, pure Snyder, and pure de Sitter limits are examined explicitly, both for the energy levels and for the wave functions, which are expressed in terms of Jacobi polynomials reducing to the generalized Laguerre polynomials of the usual Landau levels.

abstracts.value: Given a quantum adversary that queries a random oracle, how do we characterize the information that they "know"? The Compressed Oracle method of Zhandry (CRYPTO 2019) is one method that records the queries that the adversary makes; this recording serves as a representation of the information that is learned. However, a significant limitation of the Compressed Oracle method is that it may continue to store information that the adversary has "forgotten." This issue is especially pertinent in the space-bounded setting, where the adversary may uncompute information to free up space, while the information may still reside in the compressed oracle. In this work, we present a simple and interpretable framework called "Compressed Oracle Duality," which extends the Compressed Oracle method for space-bounded algorithms. By applying an isometry to the memory of a quantum adversary, we obtain a pair of compressed oracles with identical marginal distributions and classical correlations which correspond to the knowledge the adversary retains. In fact, we show that the outcome of measuring the new compressed oracle database corresponds exactly to applying the pretty-good measurement on the adversary's memory. As an application of our framework for collision search, we give a simplified proof of the recent $T^2S = Ω(N\log N)$ quantum time-space tradeoff for label-symmetric algorithms due to Magniez-Zur (arXiv:2609.10808); we also prove a stronger classical tradeoff of $TS=Ω(N\log N)$ assuming label symmetry. The proofs under our framework do not require representation theory and instead bound the mutual information between the compressed oracle pairs. This highlights both how the label symmetry assumption bypasses known proof barriers as well as the challenges that remain in achieving unconditional quantum time-space tradeoffs.

titles.title: Compressed Oracle Duality: A simple framework for knowing what quantum adversaries know

abstracts.value: A central obstacle in realizing color center cavity-QED-based quantum technologies is inhomogeneity, or disorder, among individual emitters. As the number of emitters increases, so does the complexity of the experimental data, making it difficult to quantify the present physical mechanisms of disorder. Here we introduce an artificial intelligence-driven model discovery framework in which a large language model (LLM)-based agent, equipped with tools and a structured workflow, proposes candidate Hamiltonian and Lindbladian models, generates computational tools, and quantitatively evaluates competing physical hypotheses. We apply the workflow to three previously published experimental cavity-QED datasets collected from color centers in diamond and silicon carbide. Across the experiments, the agent successfully identifies physical models for the system and characterizes the disorder. In assessing reproducibility, we find that run-to-run variability is concentrated primarily in the research plan generation step, while the computational analysis itself is substantially more consistent. Our results suggest that structured LLM agent workflows can support model discovery from quantum optical experimental data while simultaneously allowing for human expert supervision and collaboration.

abstracts.value: Constrained quantum samplers often produce infeasible outputs that retain information about good feasible solutions. We develop a post-measurement framework that constructs problem-dependent classical feasibility maps from constraint-violation statistics and pushes the raw quantum sampling law forward onto the feasible set. The probability of each repaired solution is the total raw mass of its repair preimage, enlarging the successful sampling event from a target feasible set to its full repair preimage. We derive exact identities for repaired success and expected cost, and separate repair-basin geometry from sampler-dependent probability concentration. For noisy implementations, we distinguish leakage from the encoded subspace from concentration loss within it. For permutation constraints, Hungarian maximum-overlap repair provides an O(n^3) implementation, which we study on traveling-salesman problems (TSP). We derive conditional repaired-success bounds and quantify how basin aggregation reduces the absolute-transfer budget required by these bounds. Noiseless simulations show that optimal repair basins contain selectively overweighted infeasible contributors. For an n=10 TSP instance, pushforward repair recovered the optimum using approximately 10^3 shots, compared with 10^6 shots in the original CE-QAOA workflow without repair. On a 127-qubit IBM processor, using encodings of up to 100 qubits, repaired candidates match reference tours on smaller benchmarks and improve them on larger instances. These results establish concentration of quantum probability on useful repair preimages as a design principle for constrained quantum optimization.

titles.title: Leaving Quantum Bias on the Table: Pushforwards as a Path to Quantum Advantage in Constrained Optimization

abstracts.value: Quantum circuit simulators are essential for quantum algorithm development, yet systematic runtime benchmarks comparing major frameworks across CPU and GPU backends are limited. We benchmark three open-source frameworks - Cirq (qsim), CUDA-Q, and Qiskit (Aer) - on statevector simulation of the 2D quantum acoustic wave equation, evolved via Trotterized Hamiltonian dynamics, for problem sizes from 7 to 29 qubits on a single Azure virtual machine. The evaluation spans four categories: CPU runtime versus qubit count, strong scalability on multi-core CPUs at 27 qubits, GPU runtime versus qubit count, and GPU-over-CPU speedup. Relative rankings shift from one category to the next. On CPU, Cirq is fastest up to 23 qubits (2.4x faster than Qiskit at 21 qubits), but Qiskit overtakes it at larger sizes and higher thread counts, sustaining 80% parallel efficiency at 16 threads. On GPU, CUDA-Q leads between 13 and 21 qubits, while Cirq becomes the fastest GPU backend at large problem sizes, achieving 1.5x and 2.3x speedups over CUDA-Q and Qiskit at 29 qubits. GPU-over-CPU speedup ratios should be interpreted alongside absolute GPU runtimes; CUDA-Q's 1500x at 21 qubits is largely driven by the limited scaling of its CPU backend (qpp), and the absolute GPU runtimes show that the three frameworks' GPU backends differ by less than these ratios alone suggest. These results indicate that no single framework dominates across configurations, and that backend selection for statevector simulation should be guided by both target hardware and problem size.

titles.title: Benchmark Study for Quantum Statevector Simulators for Scientific Computing

abstracts.value: We study a real scalar field nonminimally coupled to curvature on a fixed Ellis wormhole background. The scalar perturbation decouples at linear order, and the substitution $ x=a \tan z $ reduces its static radial equation to a trigonometric Pöschl-Teller problem. This yields the exact threshold spectrum $ ζ_{n\ell}=(n+\ell+1)^2/2 $, closed-form Gegenbauer profiles, and an exact count of negative radial eigenvalues in each angular sector. The s-wave thresholds are zero-energy resonances at which the growth rate rises linearly, whereas the $ \ell \geq1\ $ threshold states are square integrable and the growth rate rises as a square root. At the first threshold we also obtain the next-order term, $ σa=(π/4)g-(3π/16)g^2+O(g^3) $ with $g=2ζ-1 $. For a probe field with quartic self-interaction, we show that no nontrivial spherical static solution exists for $ζ\leq1/2 $ and derive local branch expansions near the s-wave thresholds. Numerical evolutions are consistent with saturation on the nodeless branch. These nonlinear results refer to the probe-field model; they do not establish the existence or stability of fully backreacted scalarized wormholes.

titles.title: Exact scalarization thresholds and onset laws for a nonminimally coupled scalar field on the Ellis wormhole

abstracts.value: In this note we present a detailed computation of the BPS states from M2-branes wrapping 2-cycles in local Calabi-Yau manifolds, at the level of brane quantization. The BPS states of 5d $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theories are interpreted from the local geometries, which are presented in a number of case studies. In particular, we compute the refined GV invariants for generalized conifolds, local CY3 giving 5d $\mathcal{N}=1$ gauge theories and a singularity whose crepant resolution contains a singular divisor. For the cases of local Calabi-Yau fourfolds, we point out the supersymmetric quantum mechanics is of type $\mathcal{N}=2B$. We set up the framework for studying M2-branes wrapping 2-cycles, and discuss a few cases of M2-brane wrapping genus-0 curves with this new approach.

abstracts.value: The non-Hermitian nature of black hole quasinormal modes (QNMs) can give rise to remarkable spectrum instability. Such instability is naturally characterized by the pseudospectrum for the operator. However, conventional pseudospectrum analyses permit arbitrary operator perturbations that may not correspond to physically admissible modifications. In this work, we introduce the structured pseudospectrum into black hole perturbation theory. We construct two physically motivated perturbation spaces based on effective field theory and the Rezzolla--Zhidenko parametrization, and get their structured pseudospectra using two distinct norms. Our numerical results show that imposing physical constraints substantially reduces the accessible spectrum instability, especially for higher overtones. More importantly, at sufficiently small perturbation scales $\varepsilon$, the structured pseudospectrum around isolated QNMs exhibits approximately elliptical contours with preferred directions that depend on both the mode and the perturbation space, revealing an anisotropic structure beyond the familiar circular behavior of the conventional pseudospectrum.

titles.title: The structured pseudospectrum of Schwarzschild black hole

abstracts.value: We characterize the exact error-exponent trade-off in binary quantum hypothesis testing with a rejection option for faithful states on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. The probabilities of rejection under the two hypotheses are required to vanish exponentially, with exponents at least $K$ and $L$. We show that a quadruple $(a,b,K,L)$ of positive error and rejection exponents is achievable if and only if it satisfies three single-letter conditions: two conditions involve Petz--Rényi quantities and coincide with the converse bound conjectured to be tight by Ji and Regula; the third involves the $α$--$z$ Rényi quantities on the triangle $\max\{α,1-α\}\le z\le1$. The proof combines a sector decomposition inside Schur--Weyl blocks, an explicit one-shot measurement construction, and an exact minimax argument.

abstracts.value: We introduce logics of dependence and independence over polyteams (that is, databases with multiple relation schemes), in a similar way as in arXiv:1704.02158v3 [cs.LO]. On this basis, we develop a logical framework in which we can express (in formulas) relevant properties about the statistics of a repeated quantum experiment. In this framework, we formalize Bell's theorem, and the Kochen-Specker theorem as failure of logical entailments, as it was suggested in arXiv:2107.10817v3 [math.LO]. The key feature of polyteam logics in action here is their power to express both local and global properties, with respect to the set of possible measurements. The point of this is at least twofold. Firstly, as in arXiv:1102.0264v7 [quant-ph], it gives a high-level (information-theoretic) understanding of these physical phenomena, that is not intrinsic to the physical objects involved. Secondly, since logical entailment is often (partially) axiomatizable, this framework incites us to tackle the question of contextuality computationally. We also define semiring-weighted polyteams along with logics on them, and use them to recover the probabilistic versions of the contextuality theorems mentioned above.

abstracts.value: Lieb-Robinson bounds formulate emergent causality in quantum many-body dynamics. In this Letter, we study interacting bosonic systems with long-range interactions, in which both the standard assumptions of short-range interactions and uniformly bounded local energy scales are absent. We derive upper and lower bounds whose effective light-cone exponents are governed by a nontrivial interplay between the decay exponent $α$ and the bosonic interaction order $p$. The propagation protocol concentrates bosons within blocks, creating a mediating sublattice with amplified interactions. For $p\ge4$ and $2d<α\le2d+1$, the resulting exponents coincide, determining the optimal leading light-cone power. The upper bound includes $α=2d+1$ with arbitrarily small exponent loss, using a fixed-$k$ extension of the bounded-interaction result. Our results reveal that the interplay between long-range couplings and unbounded bosonic degrees of freedom gives rise to a richer light-cone structure than in either long-range bounded systems or short-range bosonic systems alone.

abstracts.value: We develop a density-functional theory for the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian of nonrelativistic quantum electrodynamics in the spirit of the convex-analytic formulation of Lieb. We consider finitely many electrons, subject to external scalar and vector potentials, coupled to the full continuum of massless transverse photons with an ultraviolet cutoff. The natural basic variables are the standard electron density and a combined current density, the sum of the paramagnetic current density and a field-induced current density generated by the quantized vector potential. We prove representability results for these density-current pairs and show that the mixed-state constrained-search functional attains its infimum and coincides with the Lieb functional obtained by convex conjugation. Since arbitrarily soft photons purify mixed states at a negligible energy cost without changing their density and combined current density, the pure-state Levy-Lieb functional equals the Lieb functional and is therefore convex, even though its infimum need not be attained. In addition, we establish the zero-coupling limit, which recovers the mixed-state Vignale-Rasolt functional of current-density-functional theory. Finally, we consider the long-wavelength (dipole) limit and show that the limiting functional can be written as a constrained search for the well-known length-gauge dipole Hamiltonian.

abstracts.value: We study the real-time response of a Schwarzschild black hole in the Hartle-Hawking state to an external massless scalar field. In the low-frequency tidal expansion, we recover the known relation between the logarithmic running of the conservative dynamical Love coefficient at order $ω^2$ and the leading dissipative response at order $ω$.
